# ADR-1112: One local broker owns every PostgreSQL connection

## Status

accepted (owner approval of increments 1 to 6, 2026-10-21). Increments 0 to 6 are implemented on branch `fix/idle-transaction-lock`, not merged; the increment log below records each one with its measurements. Touches ADR-0479 (store lifecycle in hooks), ADR-0534 and ADR-0565 (per-process pools), ADR-0545 (hash-gated DDL on store open, superseded by decision 5), ADR-0561 (server-side decay cursor, superseded by increment 0), ADR-0637 (`python -m mcp_server.migrate`), ADR-1108 (Setup is the install step). Reuses ADR-0510, ADR-0511, ADR-0512 and `docs/provenance/capture-worker-design.md` (resident worker: private socket, kernel lease, peer credentials, bounded mailbox) and ADR-1094 (Windows has no `AF_UNIX` in CPython). Must be reconciled with the managed-PostgreSQL ADR of PR #748 (numbered 1110 there, not merged; its supervisor owns the cluster lifecycle, TCP 127.0.0.1 only).

## Context

### Incident (2026-10-20, observed with `ps` on the PostgreSQL backends)

`FATAL: sorry, too many clients already` on the store `cortex` (`max_connections = 100`): about 100 backends, 89 `SELECT/PARSE/BIND waiting`, 10 idle, one `ALTER TABLE waiting` for about 2 h, and one `idle in transaction` backend for about 2 h owned by `python -m mcp_server.hooks.consolidate_background`. SIGTERM to that process drained the queue in under 15 s. The server's lock table was not recorded during the incident; the mechanism below is reproduced from the code and captured from `pg_stat_activity`, `pg_blocking_pids` and `pg_locks` on a private cluster (`python scripts/repro_lock_chain.py`, evidence `docs/verification/connection-broker/evidence/lock-chain-*.json`), and its signature is the one `ps` showed.

### Measured causes (file:line on `main` at `df3a4479`; append-only log `docs/verification/connection-broker/experiment-log.md`)

1. **A transaction spanned a whole consolidation pass, and closed a cycle the server cannot see.** `pg_store_query_stream.py:90-104` read the corpus through a named cursor inside `conn.transaction()` on a batch-pool connection and `yield`ed between fetches. Every consumer did non-database work per row while the transaction stayed open: `consolidation/compression.py:49` (an `encode` per memory), `forgetting.py:73-86` (a neighbour search and writes per memory), `memify.py:112`, `decay.py:77`, `homeostatic.py:204,231`, `sleep.py:47`, `wiki_backlog_pass.py:68`, `consolidate.py:359`. Captured with `main`'s code (experiment `stream/main`): the consumer's stream backend is `idle in transaction` on `FETCH FORWARD 1 FROM "decay_stream"` holding a granted AccessShareLock on `memories`; the no-op `ALTER` waits for AccessExclusiveLock, `pg_blocking_pids` = the consumer; three readers wait for AccessShareLock, blocked by the `ALTER`. The consumer's own next write (`UPDATE memories SET importance ...`, interactive pool) then waits, blocked by the `ALTER`: a cycle through the client process. PostgreSQL reports no deadlock after three `deadlock_timeout` rounds and nothing moves until the reproduction script kills the consumer; the readers then complete. With this branch's code (`stream/branch`) the paused consumer holds no transaction, the `ALTER` and the readers complete at once (readers 0.006 s) and the write succeeds.
2. **Runtime processes issued DDL.** `pg_store.py:89-90` calls `_init_schema` on every `PgMemoryStore` construction; `pg_store_ddl.py:156` compared the recorded `schema_meta.ddl_hash` with the code's and, on any difference, `pg_store_ddl.py:164-178` re-applied all of `get_all_ddl()` under an advisory lock. Captured with `main`'s code (experiment `open/main`): a store opening on a database recorded at another revision logged 98 DDL statements (`log_statement = ddl`); with one client idle in a transaction that read `memories`, the first one to wait is `ALTER TABLE memories ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS is_team_decision ...` (`pg_schema.py:1397`, ADR-1083), AccessExclusiveLock not granted, blocked by the idle client, and three readers queue behind the opening store. PostgreSQL takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for ALTER TABLE unless a subform says otherwise ([ALTER TABLE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.html)); `IF NOT EXISTS` only suppresses the error. With this branch's code (`open/branch`): 0 DDL statements, the store opens while the client is idle, the readers complete in 0.008 s. Two trees labelled 4.23.5 use the live store with different DDL (log entry 2: Claude plugin `44002703...`, Codex uv-tool wheel `c8674541...`); the live `schema_meta` flipped between them within 17 minutes on 2026-10-21 (log entries 1 and 7). Reproduced with the installed Codex tree itself (experiment `flipflop/main+other`): opening `main`, the Codex tree, `main`, the Codex tree logs 0, 98, 98, 98 DDL statements and the recorded revision alternates; with this branch instead of `main` (`flipflop/branch+other`) the branch logs 0 every time and the Codex tree only once. Other runtime DDL: `handlers/backfill_helpers.py:69` (`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS backfill_log` per backfill); `infrastructure/staging_resolve_sink.py:87,104` (session-local temp tables, no shared relation).
3. **Connections scale with processes, not with work.** Each process that touches the store builds its own `PgMemoryStore`, cached per process (`memory_store.py:80`) and closed when a hook exits (ADR-0479): one persistent connection (`pg_store_schema.py:30-34`), an interactive pool of 2 to 8 (`pg_store_schema.py:53-66`, `memory_config.py:152-153`) and a batch pool of 1 to 2 (`pg_store_schema.py:68-81`, `memory_config.py:157-158`), so 1 to 11 connections per process. Hooks also open raw connections outside the store: `hooks/auto_recall.py:120`, `hooks/session_start_db.py:52`, `hooks/agent_briefing_query.py:33`; diagnostics and setup do too (`doctor.py:141,165`, `doctor_mcp.py:417,470`, `doctor_pgvector.py:41`, `migrate.py:20`, `scripts/setup_db.py`, `scripts/setup.py:343`). Processes: one MCP server per session per host (Claude Code and Codex), per-event hooks (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`: PreToolUse 2, SessionStart 1, UserPromptSubmit 1, PostToolUse 4, SessionEnd 1, Notification 1, SubagentStart 1; `plugins/hypermnesia-mcp-codex/hooks/hooks.json`: PreToolUse 3, PostToolUse 4, and others), the detached `consolidate_background` (`hooks/session_start_consolidate.py:35`, single-flight per period through the groomer coordinator), detached `session_lifecycle --consolidate` (log entry 7: two alive for 1 h 26 and 2 h 50), the resident capture worker, and cortex-viz (separate repository, same store). Live census (log entry 7): 3 to 4 TCP connections per Cortex process.
4. **Saturation reproduced in a control environment** (log entry 5 and the scripted `baseline` entries): private cluster, `max_connections = 20`, one idle reader, one queued no-op `ALTER`, 8 hook-like processes each opening a store. In each of four runs 4 or 5 of the 8 processes were refused (`FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`) or timed out on their pool after 5 s, and each blocked process held 2 to 4 connections (its pool grows while its request waits). One command: `python scripts/repro_connection_broker.py baseline`.

### State of the art and the gap

- PgBouncer: `max_client_conn`, `default_pool_size` per user/database pair, `reserve_pool_size`, `query_wait_timeout` ([config](https://www.pgbouncer.org/config.html)); no priority between clients. Transaction pooling never supports `SET/RESET`, `LISTEN`, `WITH HOLD` cursors, `PREPARE/DEALLOCATE`, temp tables with `PRESERVE/DELETE ROWS`, or session-level advisory locks; protocol-level prepared statements need `max_prepared_statements` ([features](https://www.pgbouncer.org/features.html)). Cortex uses session settings (`pg_iterative_scan.enable_iterative_scan`), session advisory locks (`pg_store_ddl.py`) and `ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS` temp tables (`staging_resolve_sink.py:87,104`).
- PgCat (Rust, MIT): transaction and session pooling "identical to PgBouncer", load balancing, sharding; in transaction mode prepared statements, `SET` and advisory locks are not supported ([repo](https://github.com/postgresml/pgcat)).
- Odyssey (C, BSD-3-Clause): multi-threaded, per-pool authentication, pool mode and limits, rolls back a disconnected client's open transaction ([repo](https://github.com/yandex/odyssey)).
- Supavisor (Elixir, Apache-2.0): cloud-native multi-tenant pooler, transaction mode only ([repo](https://github.com/supabase/supavisor)).
- Local daemons: Docker moved its control API from TCP on 127.0.0.1 to a Unix socket so that Unix permissions guard it and cross-site requests cannot reach it ([Docker security](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/)). Cortex already runs such a daemon: the capture worker (0700 directory, 0600 socket, `flock` lifetime lease, `SO_PEERCRED`/`getpeereid`, one pending mailbox for backpressure, `docs/provenance/capture-worker-design.md`).
- psycopg_pool bounds a queue with `max_waiting` (`TooManyRequests`) and a wait with `timeout` ([pool API](https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/api/pool.html)); its documentation does not state the order in which waiters are served.

Gap: every pooler above is a wire-protocol proxy. It bounds server connections but still lets each client open a transaction, hold it across its own work and issue DDL (experiment `stream/main` would run unchanged behind any of them); none offers interactive-over-background priority; all are a native binary to ship per platform. Cortex needs a bound on server connections and, by construction, no client-held transactions and no client DDL. That is an application-level broker: clients send operations, not SQL sessions.

### Alternatives rejected

- `lock_timeout` / `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` on Cortex connections: they bound a wait ([client settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html)) and leave the per-process connection count and client DDL in place; the owner rejected them as the fix (2026-10-21).
- Smaller per-process pools: lowers the constant, keeps connections proportional to processes.
- An external pooler (above): new per-platform binary, breaks session features Cortex uses, no priorities, does not remove client DDL.

## Decision

0. **Increment 0 (implemented).** Opening a store runs DDL only on a database with no recorded revision (first run); otherwise it reads the revision and warns, naming `python -m mcp_server.migrate` (`pg_store_ddl.PgDdlMixin._init_schema`). `pg_store_ddl.apply_schema` is the only DDL path (migrate, `scripts/setup_db.py`, the test fixtures). `iter_memories_for_decay` pages by `id` in autocommit, one statement per chunk on a batch-pool connection returned before the chunk is yielded: no transaction spans a `yield`. Tests: `tests_py/infrastructure/test_pg_no_runtime_ddl_no_idle_tx.py`; captured: experiments `stream/branch`, `open/branch`, `flipflop/branch+other`.
1. **One broker per store.** A resident process per resolved store (DATABASE_URL and `CORTEX_CLAUDE_DIR`) is the only Cortex code that holds PostgreSQL connections: one bounded pool of P connections. Every other Cortex process (MCP servers, hooks, consolidation, capture, doctor's store checks) talks to it. Single instance by a kernel `flock` lease and a launch lock; the creator binds, then spawns the broker with the listener and the lease inherited (`Popen(pass_fds=...)`), the capture worker's lifecycle (ADR-0512). Idle exit after 300 s (the capture worker's `CORTEX_CAPTURE_IDLE_SECONDS` default).
2. **Transport.** Unix stream socket in a 0700 directory owned by the user, socket mode 0600, kernel peer credentials checked on both sides (Linux `SO_PEERCRED`, macOS `getpeereid`), no TCP, no abstract socket, no network listener. Reuses `capture_socket`, `capture_peer`, `capture_lock`. Frames: four-byte network-order length plus one UTF-8 JSON object, size-checked before allocation (the capture protocol). Windows: CPython has no `AF_UNIX` (ADR-1094), so the second transport is a named pipe whose protected DACL grants access to the current user's SID only, created with `FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE` and `PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS`; the client checks that the serving process runs as its own SID before it sends anything (owner decision 2 below, `broker_pipe.py`).
3. **Operations, not SQL.** A request names one allowlisted store operation (the public methods of `PgMemoryStore`) with JSON arguments; no SQL text crosses the socket. Each request is one unit of work: the broker borrows a connection, runs the operation (at most one transaction, committed or rolled back inside the request) and returns the connection before answering. A client therefore never holds a transaction or a lock between requests. Streams (`iter_*`) are credit-based: the client asks for the next chunk, the broker runs the next keyset page (increment 0), nothing stays open between chunks.
4. **Queue semantics.** Two classes: interactive (recall, remember, hook reads and writes) and background (consolidation, backfill, ingest, wiki maintenance). FIFO within a class. Each class has as many execution slots as its pool has connections (increment 6): background requests use the batch pool's `POOL_BATCH_MAX`, interactive requests the interactive pool's `POOL_INTERACTIVE_MAX` (R), so background never takes an interactive connection and no request runs without one. Each class has a bounded queue; a request that finds its queue full waits for a place until its deadline, then is refused with an explicit `broker busy` error, never dropped silently (the capture mailbox rule). Deadlines come from the caller (a hook's from its `timeout` in the plugin manifest); a request whose deadline passed before dispatch is not executed. No request is replayed automatically, read or write: a channel that breaks mid-request is reported as `BrokerUnavailableError` (the write may or may not have happened, the capture worker rule) and the next request reconnects, launching a broker if none answers. Background consolidation becomes a sequence of background requests (one chunk, one batch of writes each); the single-flight per period stays with the groomer coordinator. P and R come from the pool settings (ADR-0534) and were measured in increments 4 and 6 (A1, A5).
5. **Schema only in the broker.** At start, before accepting a request, the broker applies pending migrations once under the schema advisory lock, from an ordered set of versioned migrations recorded in a `schema_version` table (version, applied_at, code revision); version 1 is today's `get_all_ddl()`. A partial failure records nothing. A database at a higher version than the broker's code is refused with an explicit message (no downgrade, no DDL). Clients contain no DDL and no connection. `schema_meta` stays readable for one release.
6. **Version skew.** The handshake carries the protocol version, the broker's code revision and the schema version it serves. A client that needs a higher schema version asks an idle broker to drain and exit, then starts its own once the lease is released; an older compatible client is served. Two installs of different revisions on one machine therefore share one broker and one schema owner instead of alternating DDL (the `flipflop` experiment becomes acceptance A3).
7. **Failure modes.** Broker crash: the kernel releases the lease; the next client launches one broker, and a failed launch is an explicit error, never a fallback to a direct connection. Stale socket: removed only while holding the lease (ADR-0512). Two launches race: the launch lock and the lease admit one. Live lease with an unusable socket: explicit failure, never a second broker. PostgreSQL restart (including PR #748's supervisor restart): the broker's pool reconnects; requests in flight fail explicitly. Broker hang: the client's deadline expires and reports it.

### Zero Trust boundary

- Local only: one Unix socket (a named pipe restricted to the user's SID on Windows), no TCP listener, no abstract-namespace socket, remote pipe clients rejected, nothing reachable from the network (decision 2). PostgreSQL itself stays on 127.0.0.1 or its own socket (PR #748: TCP 127.0.0.1 only).
- Every client authenticated on every connection: the broker reads the kernel's peer identity of each accepted connection (UID on both platforms; the peer PID where the kernel reports it, Linux `SO_PEERCRED`) and refuses any UID other than its own before reading a frame; the client checks the broker's UID the same way before sending (ADR-0510). The handshake names the client kind (server, hook, job) and its code revision; the broker logs it with the kernel identity. Same-UID code is inside the boundary; nothing in a single-user process model separates it (stated limit, shared with the capture worker).
- Least privilege in the database: a migration role (owner of the Cortex schema, DDL) used only by the broker's start-up migration step, and a runtime role with DML on Cortex tables and EXECUTE on Cortex functions, no DDL, no superuser, used by the pool. Measured before this ADR: the developer role is a superuser (`rolsuper = true`, log entry 4). Implemented in increment 6: `scripts/setup_least_privilege.py` creates both roles (for the managed cluster of PR #748, its Setup can call the same provisioning); with `CORTEX_MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL` set the broker migrates as the owner and grants the runtime role data access only; with a single `DATABASE_URL` one role does both and doctor's `database roles` check warns.

### Threat model (STRIDE, broker boundary)

| Threat | Example | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Spoofing | another local user connects to the socket; a process impersonates the broker | 0700 directory, 0600 socket, owner and mode checked before connect, kernel peer UID checked by both sides (ADR-0512/0510); same-UID code is inside the boundary |
| Tampering | modified or replayed frames; SQL injection through arguments | no SQL over the socket, operation allowlist, typed argument validation, bound parameters only; frame length and JSON validated before dispatch; writes at most once with a request id in the broker log |
| Repudiation | no record of which client did a write | the broker logs request id, kernel peer UID and PID, client kind, operation, class, outcome and duration to a private rotating log (capture worker logging pattern); no memory content in the log |
| Information disclosure | socket readable by others; DSN or password leaked | private directory and socket; the DSN never crosses the socket and is redacted in logs (existing `redact_url`); responses only to the requesting peer |
| Denial of service | one client floods the queue; a slow background job starves interactive work | bounded queue per class, reserved interactive connections, per-peer in-flight cap, deadlines, frame size limit; refusal is explicit |
| Elevation of privilege | a client obtains DDL or superuser through the broker | runtime role has no DDL; migrations run only at broker start with the migration role; no client-supplied SQL |

## Consequences

Positive: Cortex's PostgreSQL connections are bounded by P plus one migration connection at broker start, whatever the number of sessions, hooks and jobs; no Cortex client can hold a transaction or issue DDL; interactive work keeps reserved capacity during consolidation; one schema owner ends the revision flip-flop; one place to observe all database work.

Negative, known: one extra local hop and JSON (de)serialisation per operation (embeddings included), measured in increment 6 (A6: +1.9 % at p50 and +5.3 % at p95 on the benchmark's recall path); a new resident process with its own lifecycle; the whole store surface must be exposed as operations and every raw connection in hooks moved behind them; the Windows pipe transport is exercised only by the Windows CI job; cortex-viz keeps its own read-only connections until its repository migrates; same-UID malicious code is not stopped (as today).

### Acceptance (measured, one command each in `scripts/repro_connection_broker.py` or `scripts/repro_lock_chain.py`, added by the increment that implements them)

- A1: the baseline scenario with 8 and with 64 client processes leaves at most P plus 1 Cortex backends and zero refused clients.
- A2: no Cortex process other than the broker opens a PostgreSQL connection (architecture test plus a `pg_stat_activity` census by `application_name` during a full session).
- A3: no DDL statement from any client: the `open` and `flipflop` experiments log DDL only from the broker's migration step.
- A4: the `stream` experiment shows no `idle in transaction` backend and no blocked reader; during a full session with its consolidation cycle, every `idle in transaction` sample is on a broker store connection and belongs to a transaction younger than 1 s (`deadlock_timeout`'s default). Revised in increment 6, for the owner to confirm: the first wording, zero samples, also counted the broker's own transactions caught between two statements of one request (0 to 8 ms old; experiment log entry 22).
- A5: an interactive request is served within its deadline while the background queue is full.
- A6: recall latency p50 and p95 through the broker against in-process, on the release benchmark's recall path; the regression budget is set from the first measurement.

Results (the increment log has the numbers): A1 and A6 in increment 6, A2, A3 and A4 in increments 5 and 6 (`census`), A5 in increments 4 and 6 (`priority`). All six pass with the commands named there, A4 under its revised wording (entry 22). A6's p95 budget, which the test does not assert, was exceeded once on the final head under a load average of 17 to 19 from other processes (+21.6 %, entry 24).

### Research protocol, supply chain and CI (NIST SP 800-218 SSDF v1.1, OWASP)

Every measurement has a one-command reproduction (`scripts/repro_connection_broker.py`, `scripts/repro_lock_chain.py`) that appends a timestamped entry to the append-only experiment log and, for lock captures, writes the raw server-side evidence; one variable per experiment (the code tree, or the number of client processes); failed approaches are logged (entry 4). No new dependency: the broker uses the standard library (`socket`, `asyncio`, `fcntl`) and psycopg/psycopg_pool, already pinned in `uv.lock`, so no new SBOM entry arises; a release SBOM is not produced today and is the owner's call. Already in CI: ruff lint (including the selected `S110` and `S608` rules) and format, pyright, the craftsmanship gate, the fuzz workflow (`.github/workflows/fuzz.yml`), OpenSSF Scorecard with SARIF upload (`scorecard.yml`), CodeQL through GitHub's default code-scanning setup and required before merge (`SECURITY.md`), Dependabot with SHA-pinned actions, attested release builds (`release.yml`). Added by this ADR: the broker frame-decoder fuzz target (`fuzz/fuzz_broker_frame.py`, increment 3, with the deterministic local run `scripts/repro_broker_frame_fuzz.py`), the protocol abuse test against a running broker (increment 4), and the CI jobs `broker-measurements`, `test-broker-mode` and `test-pg-least-privilege` (increments 1, 5 and 6).


## Owner decisions (2026-10-21, decided)

The owner approved increments 1 to 6 and decided:

1. **Divergent installs are refused, not accommodated.** A runtime never re-applies DDL. A database whose schema is newer than the runtime's code is refused with "upgrade Cortex" (`SchemaTooNewError`); one whose `schema_meta` was rewritten by an install that does not version its schema is refused with the rebuild procedure (`SchemaTamperedError`). Rationale: the `flipflop` experiment shows that tolerating two revisions on one store re-applies 98 statements per alternate start; refusing ends the alternation at the first start of the versioned runtime. The Codex uv-tool install is rebuilt from the plugin's own commit with one command, `python3 scripts/rebuild_codex_install.py --yes` (documented in `docs/codex-plugin.md`), never run by Cortex on the user's machine.
2. **Windows transport: a named pipe whose DACL grants access to the current user's SID only**, the standard Windows local IPC, consistent with ADR-1094; Unix socket 0700/0600 with kernel peer credentials elsewhere. A Windows CI job exercises the pipe transport. Rationale: CPython on Windows has no `AF_UNIX` (ADR-1094), and a pipe's DACL plays the role of the socket file mode.
3. **The sibling worktree's work is read and integrated with attribution** (commit 4dc9f66e, worktree `fix-idle-tx-pileup`): its one idea missing here, a cross-process single-flight lock for consolidation cycles, is in increment 1 (`mcp_server/infrastructure/consolidate_lock.py`). Its `lock_timeout` on DDL is not taken (the owner rejected timeouts as the fix); its record-only-on-success rule is the same as decision 5 below.
4. **CI runs the measurements**: job `broker-measurements` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) installs the runner's PostgreSQL binaries with pgvector (`.github/actions/pg-binaries`) and runs the saturation reproduction, the role probes and the lock-chain reproduction on private clusters, keeping the evidence as an artifact.
5. **The residual DDL path is closed**: the runtime reads the schema state with one catalog query whose errors propagate; only a database with no Cortex table at all is a first run. A failed read is never taken for "no schema".

## Increment log

### Increment 1 (versioned schema, refusal, single flight, CI measurements)

- `mcp_server/infrastructure/pg_migrations.py`: `SCHEMA_VERSION = 1`, `SCHEMA_HASHES` (the DDL fingerprint of each version; a DDL change without a new version fails `test_pg_migrations.py`), `schema_version` table, `read_state`, `check_runtime`, `migrate_locked`, `apply_schema`. A migration records its version and fingerprint only when every statement succeeded (`MigrationFailedError` otherwise); the audit's probe D (docs/audits/2026-10-21-three-pillar-audit.md, E13) now ends with no `schema_version`, no `schema_meta` and `python -m mcp_server.migrate` exiting 1 (`tests_py/infrastructure/test_pg_role_probes.py`). A database migrated before this ADR (fingerprint current, no `schema_version`) opens without DDL and gets its version at the next explicit migration.
- `memory_store._try_pg_verbose` lets a `SchemaError` propagate: a schema the code cannot use never becomes a silent SQLite fallback.
- Measured (`python scripts/repro_lock_chain.py`): `open/branch` refuses with `SchemaTamperedError` and logs 0 DDL; `flipflop/branch+other` logs 0, 98, 0, 0 statements and the branch's second open is refused instead of running on the other install's schema.

- Failing statements fixed at their root (owner directive 2026-10-21; census `python scripts/repro_ddl_census.py`, experiment log entry 11). Before: 58 of 99 statements failed for a non-superuser owner without extensions (1 root cause, `vector` is an untrusted extension, plus 57 dependants), and 1 failed on a re-run with extensions present (`recall_memories()`'s `SET pg_trgm.similarity_threshold` needs pg_trgm's library loaded in the session, which a re-run never did). After: a prerequisite step before any statement creates missing extensions or stops with `MigrationPrerequisiteError` naming the administrator's command, then loads pg_trgm's library; 0 failed statements fresh and on a full re-run, for a superuser and for a non-superuser owner.


### Increment 2 (the funnel: every database access goes through the store)

- `mcp_server/infrastructure/store_operations.py`: `@store_operation` marks a function of `mcp_server.infrastructure` as a store operation; `store.call(fn, *args, pool=...)` and `store.call_batch` borrow a connection from the named pool, run it, commit after it and roll back on error (one operation, one unit of work). These names are the only ones the broker will resolve (`resolve_operation` refuses anything outside the package or unmarked). Hooks, handlers and consolidation passes now call operations; the SQL they held moved to `hook_queries`, `hook_recall_queries`, `handler_operations`, `consolidation_queries`, `wiki_handler_queries`, `wiki_mirror_apply` and the existing `pg_store_*` modules. The view DSL moved from `core` to `shared` (`wiki_view_dsl`, `wiki_view_yamlish`) so that the broker compiles a view itself and no SQL text ever travels.
- Backend checks read `store.backend` instead of probing pools; hooks emit injection receipts through the store (`emit_hook_receipt` and `insert_receipt_on_connection` retired). Hooks close the shared store at exit (`close_shared_store_on_exit`): without it, a hook process waited 5 s for each pool worker thread, about 20 s per prompt (measured by the hook-test migration on a scratch database).
- `backfill_log` is part of the schema: `SCHEMA_VERSION = 2`. A version-1 database is refused at runtime (`SchemaBehindError`) and brought to version 2 by the migration step (`test_a_version_1_database_is_refused_at_runtime_then_migrated`).
- Acceptance (`python scripts/repro_store_funnel.py`, experiment log): on `main`, 59 lines in 42 files outside `infrastructure/` reach a store's connection or pools and 3 hooks import the driver; on the branch, 0 and 0. `tests_py/architecture/test_store_funnel.py` keeps both at zero and checks that every function handed to `store.call` is a marked operation.


### Increment 3 (the broker process and its transports)

- Process: `mcp_server/hooks/store_broker.py`, started by the first client that finds no broker for its store (`broker_endpoint.broker_store`), through the plugin launcher (`store_broker_launch.py`, issue #667) and detached (ADR-1102). The database URL reaches it in its environment, never its command line (`test_the_database_url_is_not_on_the_command_line`). At start it runs the migration step, then serves; it exits after `CORTEX_BROKER_IDLE_SECONDS` (default 300) with no connection and no work, removing its socket.
- Unix transport (`broker_unix.py`): the capture worker's endpoint reused as is, in an owner-only directory per store, `<Cortex root>/.store-broker/<16 hex of sha256(URL)>`; launch lock, kernel lease inherited by the broker, stale socket replaced only under the lease, kernel peer UID checked on both sides before any frame. Windows transport (`broker_pipe.py`): see decision 2; the pipe name is the lease.
- Protocol (`broker_protocol.py`, `broker_codec.py`): four-byte length plus one JSON object, size-checked before allocation; `hello`/`welcome` carry protocol, code revision, schema version and the broker's PID; values outside JSON travel with a closed set of tags (timestamps, bytes, numeric arrays of twelve named dtypes, tuples, sets, non-string keys, decimals, UUIDs, and dataclasses or named tuples of `mcp_server` modules already imported, never imported by a frame). No pickle, no SQL.
- Dispatch (`broker_executor.py`, `broker_scheduler.py`, `broker_server.py`): a request names an allowlisted store method (public, not lending a connection, not a generator; plus the keyset page of increment 0) or a marked operation; two classes with reserved interactive capacity, bounded queues, deadlines, refusal at the caller's deadline, no execution after an expired deadline. P, R and the session bounds are increment 4.
- Version skew (decision 6): a client that needs a newer schema asks the broker to drain; a broker on a newer schema is refused by an older client with "upgrade Cortex" (`broker_client.py`).
- `schema_versions.py`: the versions, refusals and runtime check moved out of `pg_migrations` so that clients without the PostgreSQL driver (the Windows CI job, the broker's clients) can compare versions.
- Tests: codec and frames (`test_broker_codec.py`), queues (`test_broker_scheduler.py`), server and client over connected sockets (`test_broker_server.py`), endpoint (`test_broker_unix.py`: per-store directory, foreign peer closed before any frame, live lease without a socket never starts a second broker, stale socket replaced), real processes on the test database (`test_store_broker_process.py`: first spawn and reuse, 8 concurrent first requests start one broker, crash then relaunch with the broken request reported and not replayed, idle exit), pipe (`test_broker_pipe.py`, in the `test-windows` job: DACL read back from a live pipe holds one ACE, the user's; a second broker cannot take the name; a request round-trips).
- Fuzz: `fuzz/fuzz_broker_frame.py` (ClusterFuzzLite) and `python scripts/repro_broker_frame_fuzz.py` (local, deterministic): the first decoder let 234 of 20000 mutated frames escape with exceptions other than `ProtocolError`; after typed field checks, 0 of 2.2 million (experiment log entry 13).


### Increment 4 (request classes reach the database; session bounds; A5)

- The request class is a context of the store work (`store_operations.request_class`, `current_request_class`): the broker sets it from each request, `@background_work` sets it for the batch tool handlers (consolidate, backfill_memories, codebase_analyze, ingest_codebase, ingest_document, import_sessions, seed_project, rebuild_profiles). Background work runs every store statement on the batch pool (`PgDdlMixin._execute`, `StoreOperationsMixin.call` without an explicit pool), so the database itself sees the reservation: at most `POOL_BATCH_MAX` connections for background, `POOL_INTERACTIVE_MAX` kept for interactive work.
- P and R: one broker holds at most P = 1 + `POOL_INTERACTIVE_MAX` + `POOL_BATCH_MAX` = 11 connections (defaults, ADR-0534); its scheduler ran 10 workers, 8 reserved for interactive requests and background capped at 2 (`store_broker_policy.server_policy`); increment 6 replaced this with per-class slots after A1 measured pool timeouts. Measured with these values (A5 below); A1 counts the backends in increment 6.
- Session bounds (`pg_session_bounds.py`; audit Track 0.2, probe A), backstops and not the fix: every store connection is named `cortex-store-<pool>-<pid>` (the PID suffix since the end of increment 4, so a census attributes each backend to its process) and carries `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout` equal to its class deadline (interactive 30 s, batch 30 min) and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` of 30 s. Main had 0, 0, 0 and an empty name (audit E10). `python scripts/repro_connection_broker.py bounds`.
- A5 (`python scripts/repro_connection_broker.py priority`, `test_broker_priority_repro.py`, CI job `broker-measurements`): one broker process on a private cluster, 20000 memories, 32 clients looping on 5000-row keyset pages against a queue of 8, one client timing point reads for 8 s. One variable, the class of the heavy load. As background: point reads p50 1.6 ms, p95 107.6 ms, max 225.4 ms (329 reads), background still served 54 pages. Sent as interactive (one FIFO): 2 point reads in 8 s, p50 8452 ms, max 9165 ms.
- Abuse on a live broker (`test_abusive_peers_are_dropped_and_the_broker_keeps_serving`): garbage, an oversized header, a wrong protocol and 200 connections beyond the client cap are dropped or refused by the kernel backlog; the established client is served by the same broker.


### Increment 5 (clients move to the broker)

- The store factory (`memory_store._open_pg`) returns a `BrokerStore` connected at once (`broker_store` launches the broker if none answers), so the MCP servers, the Claude and Codex hooks, the background jobs, the capture worker and every tool handler reach PostgreSQL only through the broker. `CORTEX_STORE_IN_PROCESS=1` holds the store in process: set by the launcher in the broker itself and by the test suite's default run. `PgMemoryStore` is built only by the broker and by that gated path (`tests_py/architecture/test_store_funnel.py::test_no_lower_layer_builds_a_shared_store`: no infrastructure, core or shared module builds a store through the factory, so the broker never connects to itself).
- Explicit errors (decision 7): a broker that cannot open the store answers every handshake with `refused` and the failure's type and message, then exits; the client raises the same `SchemaError` subclass an in-process store raised ("upgrade Cortex") or `BrokerRefusedError`. A broker that dies before answering is reported as `BrokerUnavailableError` with the end of its start-up output (`broker.out`, owner-only, next to its socket). `BrokerLaunchError` and `BrokerUnavailableError` are never turned into a SQLite fallback. Built-in exception types raised in the broker are raised again as themselves in the client (`broker_errors.remote_error`).
- One broker per resolved store: the key is a digest of the URL and the Cortex root. A socket path longer than `sun_path` (103 bytes) moves to `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/cortex-<uid>` or the resolved `/tmp/cortex-<uid>`, created owner-only and checked like every parent (a base writable by others is refused).
- Doctor: `store broker` check, running PID or "not running, the first client starts it", never starting one (`doctor_broker.py`).
- The suite in broker mode (`CORTEX_TEST_BROKER_MODE=1`, CI job `test-broker-mode`): first run 40 failed and 40 errors of 10387 collected. Causes: no surface or codec gap in production beyond one private helper (`store._now_iso()` in `core/write_post_store.py`, replaced) and the socket path length above; the rest were tests reaching the store's own connection or class. Resolution, counted: 24 test modules and 1 test that test the store itself (its connections, its pools, its class, or a log line emitted where the operation runs) are marked `in_process_store` and run on the in-process store in both modes; 8 test files read or seed rows through `tests_py/_db_peek.store_connection` (the store's connection in process, a direct connection through the broker); 1 test (a mid-session process-table assertion) is skipped in broker mode because the session's broker is alive by design. Final: default 10336 passed, 27 skipped; broker mode 10335 passed, 28 skipped.
- A2 and A4 (`python scripts/repro_connection_broker.py census`, CI job `broker-measurements`): a scripted session of real processes on a private cluster with 5000 memories (SessionStart, three UserPromptSubmit recalls, one `remember`, one `consolidate`) and a `pg_stat_activity` sampler every 50 ms: every Cortex backend carries one PID, the broker's; no other client backend; 0 `idle in transaction` samples in 284; at most 6 Cortex backends. First hook 1.12 s (it starts the broker), next hooks 0.44 to 0.51 s.

### Increment 6 (per-process pools gone, roles split, A1 and A6)

- Per-process pools: since increment 5 no client process builds a `PgMemoryStore`, so the interactive and batch pools exist only in the broker (or in a process that runs the store in process on purpose: the broker, the tests). `test_only_the_broker_and_the_gated_factory_build_a_pg_store` pins the two construction sites.
- Roles (Zero Trust boundary; audit Track 0.3, probe B): `scripts/setup_least_privilege.py` (one command, as an administrator) creates a migration role that owns the database and a runtime role with CONNECT only, the extensions, and revokes CREATE on `public` from PUBLIC. The broker migrates with `CORTEX_MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL` and then grants the role of `DATABASE_URL` data access only: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on the tables and views of `public` and `wiki`, USAGE, SELECT, UPDATE on their sequences, EXECUTE on their functions (`pg_roles.grant_runtime`, after each migration, so a table a migration adds is usable at the same start). Probe B (`test_pg_least_privilege_probe_b.py`): with that runtime role the `remember` and `recall` handlers work through the broker; the runtime role cannot create a table before or after the grants; every table belongs to the migration role. On main the runtime role could not open the store (audit E12).
- E14 fixed at its root: `recall_memories()` declared `SET pg_trgm.similarity_threshold = '0.1'`, which a non-superuser cannot create before pg_trgm is loaded in the session (measured on a private cluster: `InsufficientPrivilege`). Schema version 3 sets the threshold in the function body with `set_config(..., true)` and restores the caller's value before returning (`test_function_plan_policy_does_not_change_the_callers_setting` and `test_trigram_between_point_one_and_session_default` keep pinning that the caller's setting is untouched); the library-loading step of increment 1 is gone with it. `python scripts/repro_least_privilege_suite.py` runs the whole suite as a role with LOGIN and CREATEDB only (CI job `test-pg-least-privilege`).
- A1 found two defects, both fixed (experiment log entries 17 and 18). The store opened its pools lazily without a lock, so the broker's worker threads each opened a pool on first use: 12 to 16 interactive connections from a pool of 8; pool creation is now double-checked under a per-store lock (`test_pg_pool_once.py` fails without it). The scheduler let interactive requests use 10 workers for 8 interactive connections, so with 8 reads blocked behind the `ALTER` two more timed out in the pool (6 of 64 clients failed); each class now has exactly as many slots as its pool has connections, and a request waits in the broker's queue, bounded by its deadline, never in the pool.
- A1 (`python scripts/repro_connection_broker.py saturation`): the baseline scenario (private cluster, `max_connections = 20`, one idle reader, one queued no-op `ALTER`) with 8 and with 64 clients reaching the store through the broker: 9 Cortex backends at peak (P plus 1 is 12), one PID, 0 refused, 0 failed, every client served once the reader ends its transaction. Main: 4 or 5 of 8 refused, 2 to 4 connections per blocked client.
- A5 re-run with per-class slots (`priority`): point reads p50 2.0 ms, p95 110.0 ms while 32 clients saturate the background queue; 1 read in 8 s (9900 ms) when the same load shares one class.
- A6 (`python scripts/repro_connection_broker.py latency`): the release benchmark's recall path (`pg_recall.recall`, the call `BenchmarkDB.recall` makes) on 3000 memories, 150 queries, neural embeddings, rerank off on both sides: in process p50 215.5 ms, p95 262.3 ms; through the broker p50 219.6 ms, p95 276.3 ms. Parity before any write, each broker call bracketed by two in-process calls, with a second in-process store as the control arm: 3 of 150 rankings differ through the broker, 3 of 150 through the control, so the broker adds no difference of its own. Regression budget, set from this first measurement: broker p95 within 10 % of in-process p95. `benchmarks/reproduce.sh` itself was not run: it starts its PostgreSQL in Docker, and the Docker daemon is not running on this machine; the transport is the one variable A6 changes, and the scoring code is identical on both sides.
- A3 (`census`, now with `log_statement = ddl` on its cluster): 0 DDL statements on shared relations during the whole session; the same log holds the 103 statements of the setup's migration before it, so the instrument records DDL. Clients hold no connection (A2), so only the broker's start-up migration could issue DDL, and on a current schema it applies none.
- Doctor reports whether migration and runtime run as two roles (`database roles`), and warns when one role does both.
- Census follow-up (experiment log entry 22): on the clean head the census failed once on a client backend with an empty name, unattributed under a names-only instrument and absent from the 28 runs recorded since; the broker's migration and grant connections, which had no name, are now `cortex-migrate-<pid>`, and the sampler records pid, ages and query head of anything unattributed. A4's first wording failed in 4 runs, one sample each: the broker's interactive transactions caught between two statements (`SET LOCAL jit = off`, then the recall), 0 to 7 ms old; A4 now asserts that every such sample is the broker's and younger than 1 s. Each census session also starts a detached consolidation cycle; the census now waits for the session's detached processes with the sampler on. Ten runs after the change: 10 passed, one broker PID, 0 other backends, at most one idle sample per run (8 ms).
- Final head (experiment log entry 24, load average 17 to 19 from processes outside this work): census passes (one broker PID, 0 other backends, 0 idle samples), A1 passes (9 backends, 0 failed), A5 passes (point reads p95 88.0 ms); A6 parity holds (1 of 150 through the broker, 3 through the control), p50 +1.9 %, p95 +21.6 % (493.5 ms in process, 600.2 ms through the broker), outside the 10 % budget. A run on an unloaded machine, or the CI job, is the next measurement; whether the budget becomes an assertion is the owner's decision.
- Suites at the end of increment 6: default (store in process) 10343 passed, 29 skipped; through the broker 10342 passed, 30 skipped; as a role without SUPERUSER 10345 passed, 27 skipped (experiment log entry 23).
